Family Health

Secondary syphilis: symptoms, testing and treatment

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Secondary syphilis is a stage of infection caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum. It can cause a widespread rash, mouth or genital lesions and symptoms that resemble many other illnesses. The infection is treatable, but a rash fading or a sore healing does not mean it has gone away. Testing, the right antibiotic treatment and follow-up are needed, including attention to partners and any pregnancy.

How secondary syphilis fits into the stages

Syphilis is commonly described in four stages: primary, secondary, latent and tertiary. These describe patterns of illness over time, but an individual may not recognise every stage. Symptoms can be mild, hidden or mistaken for another condition.

The primary stage usually involves a sore, called a chancre, where infection entered the body. Secondary symptoms can begin while that sore is healing or several weeks afterwards. They do not follow an exact two-to-eight-week timetable in every person.

If untreated, the infection can enter a latent stage with no visible symptoms and remain in the body for years. Some people later develop tertiary disease with damage to organs. The absence of a rash is therefore not proof that treatment is unnecessary.

Neurosyphilis is not another name for tertiary syphilis. Infection involving the nervous system, eyes or ears can occur at any stage, including early disease. These complications require specific assessment and treatment.

The first sore may have been easy to miss

A primary sore often appears about three weeks after exposure, although the interval can be much shorter or longer. WHO describes a range of roughly nine to ninety days. That variation is one reason the date a sore appears cannot identify an exact date of infection.

The sore is often firm, round and painless. It may be on the genitals, around or inside the anus, or on the lips or inside the mouth. There can be more than one sore, and not every lesion has the classic painless appearance.

A hidden or painless sore may go unnoticed. It can heal over several weeks without treatment, but the bacteria remain. Someone may first seek care for a later rash without remembering any earlier ulcer.

Arrange a sexual-health assessment for an unexplained genital, anal or oral sore, especially after a possible exposure. Do not wait for a typical photograph-like appearance or for secondary symptoms to develop.

What the secondary rash can look like

A secondary rash may affect several parts of the body, including the palms and soles. It is often described as red or reddish-brown, rough or slightly raised, although colour and visibility vary with skin tone. Some lesions look flat, scaly or so faint that they are easily overlooked.

The rash usually does not itch, but that characteristic alone cannot confirm or exclude syphilis. Other skin conditions can look similar, and a person does not have to have a rash on both hands and feet to need testing.

Moist, broad, wart-like lesions can develop in genital or other skin folds. These syphilis lesions are called condylomata lata. Their appearance can be confused with other causes, including genital warts, but they are not simply another name for HPV infection.

There may also be lesions in the mouth or genital area. Because appearances vary and some lesions are infectious, a clinician should examine them and choose suitable tests. Avoid using a rash cream or an online image comparison as a substitute for assessment.

Other symptoms during the secondary stage

Fever, a sore throat, enlarged lymph nodes, headache, tiredness and muscle aches can accompany the skin changes. Some people also notice reduced appetite, weight loss, joint discomfort or patchy hair loss.

These symptoms overlap with many common illnesses. Their presence does not establish syphilis, but a recent sore, rash or possible sexual exposure is useful information to share with the clinician. You do not need to have every symptom on a list.

Symptoms may settle without antibiotics and can sometimes recur. That improvement should not be interpreted as the body having reliably cleared the infection. The next step remains testing and treatment when indicated.

A sexual-health service can usually assess these concerns confidentially. Seeking care is a practical health decision, not a judgment about a person’s character, relationship or sexual identity.

How infection passes between people

Syphilis commonly spreads through direct contact with an infectious sore or lesion during vaginal, anal or oral sex. Lesions can be in places that are not obvious to either partner. Early symptomatic stages are particularly important for sexual transmission.

The infection can also pass from a pregnant person to the baby during pregnancy. This can occur even when the parent has no obvious symptoms. Preventing congenital syphilis depends on timely testing and appropriate treatment, not waiting for a visible rash.

Ordinary contact with a toilet seat, doorknob, swimming pool, bathtub, clothing or shared eating utensils is not how syphilis is acquired. A diagnosis is not a reason to isolate someone from everyday household contact.

Condoms and other barriers reduce exposure during sex, but they may not cover every lesion. A sore outside the covered area can still transmit infection. Barriers are useful prevention tools, not a guarantee that contact with an infectious lesion is safe.

Why HIV and other STI testing may be offered

A syphilis sore can create a break in the skin through which HIV enters more easily. Some circumstances that create an opportunity for one sexually transmitted infection also create exposure to another. Having syphilis does not mean that someone necessarily has HIV.

An HIV test is recommended when primary or secondary syphilis is diagnosed. A clinic may also offer tests for other sexually transmitted infections according to the type and timing of exposure. If an exposure was recent, the clinician may discuss when repeat tests are needed.

People who test negative for HIV may be offered information about HIV prevention, including PrEP where appropriate. This is a separate prevention discussion; syphilis antibiotics do not protect against HIV.

Testing and support should be based on individual exposure and health needs. Being part of a population with a higher reported rate does not establish a diagnosis, and absence from such a group does not mean testing is unnecessary.

How syphilis is diagnosed

The clinician asks about symptoms, previous tests or treatment, possible exposure and pregnancy, and may examine the skin, mouth and genital or anal area. A sample from a lesion may be tested where suitable laboratory methods are available.

Direct tests can sometimes identify the organism in lesion material, using methods such as dark-field microscopy or molecular testing. Availability and the appropriate specimen vary. Most routine assessments also use blood tests.

Blood testing generally combines two types of test. A nontreponemal test, such as RPR or VDRL, measures antibodies that can help assess disease activity and follow the response. A treponemal test looks for antibodies more specifically associated with the infection.

An RPR result alone is not a definitive diagnosis. Some results can be falsely positive, and early infection can initially test negative. Treponemal antibodies can remain detectable after successful treatment. The clinician interprets the combination with the history and may arrange repeat testing.

Tell the clinic if you have been treated before and bring previous results if available. This helps distinguish a new infection, a treated infection with persistent antibodies and a result that needs further clarification.

When neurological, eye or hearing symptoms change the assessment

New visual changes, eye pain, hearing loss, severe headache, weakness, altered sensation or confusion need prompt medical attention. Syphilis is one possible cause in someone with the infection, but other urgent causes must also be considered.

A lumbar puncture, which samples cerebrospinal fluid, may be needed when neurological findings suggest nervous-system involvement. It is not a routine test for everyone with a secondary rash or a synonym for diagnosing a late stage.

Eye and ear symptoms need specialist assessment. Some people with confirmed ocular or isolated auditory disease do not need a lumbar puncture before treatment; that decision depends on examination findings. Treatment should not be delayed while a patient tries to determine which category applies.

Possible stroke symptoms, sudden major loss of vision or acute neurological changes need emergency care. Tell the treating team about any positive syphilis test or recent treatment so it can inform the assessment.

Treatment can cure the infection

Syphilis is treated with an appropriate antibiotic, most often a specific penicillin preparation. For uncomplicated primary or secondary syphilis in a nonpregnant adult, a single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G is a standard regimen. The clinician must first establish the stage and check for circumstances that change treatment.

Later infection, infection of uncertain duration, pregnancy and nervous-system, eye or ear involvement may require a different schedule or additional treatment. Penicillin products are not all interchangeable, and an antibiotic left over from another illness is not an adequate substitute.

If a nonpregnant person has a confirmed penicillin allergy, a clinician may consider an alternative such as doxycycline or tetracycline with careful follow-up. Suitability depends on the clinical situation and the ability to complete the course. Do not choose an alternative without specialist advice.

There is no over-the-counter medicine, supplement or home remedy that replaces antibiotic treatment. Completing treatment can eliminate the infection, but it may not reverse damage that occurred before treatment, such as certain neurological or sensory problems.

Ask what you will receive, what to do if a dose or visit is missed, and when follow-up tests are due. A disappearing rash is not a reliable test of whether the treatment was sufficient.

Pregnancy needs prompt, specific care

Untreated maternal infection can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, premature birth or infection in the baby. A newborn may initially look well and still need assessment and treatment. Congenital infection can later cause serious developmental, hearing, eye or other health problems.

Penicillin is the only treatment with established effectiveness for treating fetal infection and preventing congenital syphilis. A pregnant person who reports penicillin allergy needs specialist evaluation; when indicated, supervised desensitisation allows penicillin treatment.

Do not substitute doxycycline or another nonpregnancy regimen on your own. Treatment depends on the stage, and the obstetric and infection teams may recommend additional measures. A partner’s treatment does not replace treatment for the pregnant person.

Attend the recommended prenatal screening and any repeat tests advised under local guidance or because of new exposure. Tell the maternity team promptly about a positive result, a partner’s diagnosis or symptoms suggesting syphilis. The benefits of treatment should not be delayed because of fear of a temporary treatment reaction.

A temporary reaction after starting antibiotics

Within the first twenty-four hours of treatment, some people develop a Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction. Fever, chills, headache, muscle aches and a temporary worsening of the rash can occur; nausea or a general feeling of being unwell may accompany them.

This is an inflammatory response to treatment, not automatically an allergy to penicillin. It often settles within about a day, but the clinician should explain what to expect and whom to contact. Do not assume that every symptom after an injection is harmless.

Hives, swelling of the mouth or throat, wheezing, breathing difficulty or collapse can indicate a severe allergic reaction and need emergency care. A very high fever, rapidly worsening illness, chest symptoms or confusion also warrants urgent assessment rather than self-diagnosis as a routine reaction.

During pregnancy, fever, contractions or reduced fetal movement after treatment should prompt immediate obstetric advice. A possible reaction is not a reason to leave syphilis untreated. Ask the maternity team how to obtain help and whether any additional observation is needed.

Partners, sex and follow-up after treatment

Current and relevant recent partners need to be informed, assessed and sometimes treated even if they feel well or an early test is negative. The period covered depends on the stage and exposure history. A sexual-health service can help with confidential partner notification, including options that do not identify you.

Avoid vaginal, anal and oral sex until you and your partner or partners have completed the required treatment and the clinic’s waiting period, and any sores have healed. Local advice can differ; for example, the NHS advises waiting two weeks after both people finish treatment. Ask the treating service for the rule that applies to you.

Follow-up blood tests check the response rather than relying on the disappearance of symptoms. CDC guidance for primary and secondary syphilis includes clinical and serological review at six and twelve months; some situations require closer or additional follow-up.

The clinician compares quantitative test results with the pretreatment result and your history. Antibody levels do not always become negative immediately, and some specific antibodies remain for life. A persistent positive test is not by itself proof that treatment failed.

New symptoms or another exposure should be reported even after successful treatment. Having had syphilis does not provide reliable immunity; you can acquire it again. Keep a record of the diagnosis, treatment and results for future care.

Reducing future risk and recognising why treatment matters

Using condoms or appropriate barriers consistently, testing when recommended and ensuring partners receive care all help reduce transmission. Because barriers may not cover every lesion, avoid sexual contact when infection is suspected or while treatment restrictions apply.

Screening recommendations depend on local guidance, pregnancy, exposure and individual risk. A new partner, a partner’s diagnosis or a relevant symptom can justify a discussion about testing. You do not need to wait until you feel ill.

Without treatment, infection may remain silent for years and can eventually damage the heart and blood vessels, nervous system, bones, joints or other organs. Possible consequences include impaired movement, sensory loss, cognitive changes and, in severe cases, death. Not everyone develops tertiary disease, but its possibility is a reason to treat early.

Late disease is not simply untreatable. Antibiotics can still treat infection, while the extent to which established injury improves varies. Early diagnosis offers the best opportunity to prevent complications and protect partners and a pregnancy.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC guidance distinguishes the clinical stages, combined blood-test interpretation and treatment for early disease from the specific pathways for pregnancy or neurological, eye and ear involvement. A single symptom or antibody result cannot establish the whole diagnosis.

Patient guidance supports prompt treatment, partner care and repeat testing. Exact follow-up and sexual-contact restrictions should come from the treating service; references are relevant topic guidance rather than a section-by-section copy of the source article.

How BeMama can help

Keep your treatment record and follow-up appointments, and ask the clinic to explain partner notification and when sexual contact can resume. If pregnancy is possible, make that clear at the first assessment.

When to seek help

Seek prompt assessment for suspected syphilis, especially during pregnancy. Sudden neurological or visual symptoms, severe allergy signs or acute deterioration need emergency care. Do not replace prescribed treatment with a home remedy or a different antibiotic.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Secondary syphilis can cause a varied rash and general symptoms; symptoms fading does not mean infection is cured.
  • Diagnosis usually combines examination and two types of blood test, interpreted with previous treatment and exposure.
  • Appropriate antibiotics cure infection, but established damage may not fully reverse.
  • Pregnancy and neurological, eye or ear symptoms need specific treatment pathways.
  • Partners, follow-up tests and the clinic’s advice about sex remain important after treatment.

Frequently asked questions

Can secondary syphilis occur without a remembered sore?

Yes. The first sore can be painless, hidden or mistaken for something else. A person may notice the secondary rash or general symptoms without remembering the primary stage.

Does a rash on my palms or soles prove that I have syphilis?

No. It is a recognised pattern, but several conditions can cause similar changes. Syphilis can also produce other rash patterns. A clinician needs to assess the symptoms and arrange appropriate tests.

If the rash disappears, do I still need treatment?

Yes, if syphilis is diagnosed or the clinic recommends treatment after an exposure. Symptoms may disappear while the infection remains and enters a symptom-free stage. Improvement alone does not show that it has cleared.

Is one positive RPR test enough to diagnose it?

Not usually on its own. Clinicians interpret RPR or VDRL alongside a treponemal test, symptoms and previous treatment. Early infection can test negative, and some antibody tests remain positive after successful treatment.

Is neurosyphilis always a late stage?

No. Nervous-system, eye or ear involvement can occur at any stage. New neurological, visual or hearing symptoms need prompt assessment and may require a different treatment approach.

Does everyone need a lumbar puncture?

No. It is considered when findings suggest particular complications, especially neurological involvement. It is not routine for an uncomplicated secondary rash. Eye and ear symptoms require specialist decisions based on examination.

Can syphilis be treated during pregnancy if I am allergic to penicillin?

Yes, but specialist care is essential. Penicillin is the established treatment for fetal infection and prevention of congenital syphilis. A reported allergy is assessed, and supervised desensitisation may be needed before penicillin is given.

Is fever after the first injection a penicillin allergy?

Not necessarily. A Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction can cause fever and aches during the first day. Breathing difficulty, throat swelling, hives with systemic symptoms or collapse may signal a severe allergy and require emergency care. Ask for help if you are unsure or very unwell.

When can we have sex again?

Follow your clinic’s instructions after both you and relevant partners complete treatment, and wait for sores to heal. The NHS advises two weeks after both people finish treatment, but local guidance may differ. Feeling better immediately after treatment is not permission to resume contact.

Can I catch syphilis again after treatment?

Yes. Previous infection does not provide reliable immunity. Partner care, barriers and testing when indicated remain important. Keep your old treatment results because they can help a clinician interpret later blood tests.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
